questions.q: For a wave of speed $v$, frequency $f$ and wavelength $\lambda$:
questions.solution:
$v = \mathbf{f\lambda}$.

When a wave enters a new medium its **frequency is unchanged** — it is set by the source — so a change in speed forces a change in wavelength.

questions.q: The intensity of a wave is proportional to:
questions.solution:
$I \propto A^{2}$.

Doubling the amplitude gives **four times** the intensity. Intensity also falls as $\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$ from a point source, since the energy spreads over a sphere.

Only a **transverse** wave has a vibration direction across its line of travel that can be filtered.

Sound, being longitudinal, cannot be polarised — which is how it was established that light is transverse.

questions.q: In a stationary wave, the distance between adjacent nodes is:
questions.solution:
Adjacent nodes are $\mathbf{\dfrac{\lambda}{2}}$ apart, and so are adjacent antinodes.

A node and its neighbouring antinode are $\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$ apart.

questions.q: Two sources are coherent if they have:
questions.solution:
Coherence requires the **same frequency** and a **constant phase difference**.

Without it the interference pattern shifts faster than it can be observed and blurs into uniform illumination — which is why Young fed both slits from a single source.
options: a constant phase difference and the same frequency

questions.q: A wave of frequency $500$ Hz has wavelength $0.68$ m. Find its speed, in m/s.
questions.solution: $v = f\lambda = 500 \times 0.68 = \mathbf{340}$ m/s — the speed of sound in air.

questions.q: In a double-slit experiment, $\lambda = 600$ nm, $d = 0.5$ mm and $D = 2$ m. Find the fringe spacing, in mm.
A grating has $500$ lines per mm. Find the slit spacing, in nm.
questions.solution:
$d = \dfrac{1\text{ mm}}{500} = 2 \times 10^{-6}$ m $= \mathbf{2000}$ nm.

The spacing is only a few wavelengths of light, which is exactly why a grating diffracts so strongly.

questions.q: A stationary wave on a string has nodes $0.4$ m apart. Find the wavelength, in m.
questions.solution: Node spacing is half a wavelength, so $\lambda = \mathbf{0.8}$ m.

questions.q: Two points on a wave are $\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$ apart. Find the phase difference in degrees.
questions.solution: A full wavelength is $360°$, so a quarter is $\mathbf{90°}$ (or $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radians).

questions.q: Derive the fringe spacing formula for a double-slit experiment, and explain what each of the conditions on the apparatus is for.
questions.solution:
**Set-up.** Two slits $d$ apart, a screen $D$ away, and $x$ measured on the screen from the central fringe.

**Path difference.** For $D \gg d$, the two paths are nearly parallel and

$\Delta = d\sin\theta \approx d\tan\theta = \dfrac{dx}{D}$

**Bright fringes** need the path difference to be a whole number of wavelengths:

$\dfrac{dx}{D} = n\lambda \Rightarrow x_{n} = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}$

**Fringe spacing** — the gap between consecutive bright fringes:

$\mathbf{x = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}}$

**What each condition is for.**

• **Coherent sources** — otherwise the pattern shifts and blurs away. Achieved by illuminating both slits from one source.

• **Narrow slits** — so that each diffracts widely enough for the two beams to overlap.

• **Slits close together** — $d$ is in the denominator, so a small $d$ gives wider, measurable fringes.

• **Large $D$** — again to widen the fringes.

• **Monochromatic light** — each wavelength makes its own set of fringes, and white light gives coloured, overlapping bands beyond the first few.

**The historical importance.** Fringes can only arise from **superposition**, which particles cannot do. Young's experiment settled the wave nature of light — and, when repeated with single photons and electrons, became the central puzzle of quantum mechanics.

questions.q: Explain how a stationary wave is formed, describe its features, and compare it with a progressive wave.
questions.solution:
**Formation.** Two waves of the **same frequency and amplitude** travel in **opposite directions** along the same line and superpose.

In practice this is usually a wave and its own reflection from a fixed end.

**Features.**

• **Nodes** — points of permanently zero displacement, where the two waves always cancel. Spaced $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ apart.

• **Antinodes** — points of maximum oscillation, where they always reinforce. Also $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ apart, midway between nodes.

• All points **between** two nodes vibrate **in phase**, though with different amplitudes; on opposite sides of a node they are exactly out of phase.

**Comparison with a progressive wave.**

• **Energy:** transferred along the wave | stored, not transferred

• **Amplitude:** the same for every point | varies from zero at a node to a maximum at an antinode

• **Phase:** changes continuously along the wave | constant between adjacent nodes, reversing across each node

• **Waveform:** moves along | stays put

**Why no energy is transferred.** A node never moves, so no energy can cross it. The energy sloshes between kinetic and potential within each loop.

**Where they occur:** a guitar string, an organ pipe, a microwave oven (the hot spots are antinodes, which is why the turntable exists), and the standing wave patterns that determine the allowed energy levels of an electron in an atom.

questions.q: Derive $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ for a diffraction grating, and explain why a grating gives sharper maxima than a double slit.
questions.solution:
**Derivation.** Parallel light falls normally on a grating of slit spacing $d$. Consider the rays leaving at angle $\theta$ from adjacent slits.

The path difference between them is $d\sin\theta$.

For constructive interference this must be a whole number of wavelengths:

$\mathbf{d\sin\theta = n\lambda}$

where $n$ is the order of the maximum.

**Note $\sin\theta \le 1$**, so only orders up to $n = \dfrac{d}{\lambda}$ exist — a grating cannot produce arbitrarily many.

**Why the maxima are sharper.** With **two** slits, moving slightly off the exact angle leaves the two beams only slightly out of step, so the intensity falls gradually — broad fringes.

With **thousands** of slits, a small change in angle puts the outermost slits many wavelengths out of step with the first. Their contributions cancel in pairs almost completely, and the intensity collapses.

So the maxima are **very narrow and very bright**, with almost complete darkness between them.

**The practical consequence.** A grating separates wavelengths precisely, which is why spectrometers use gratings rather than prisms or double slits.

Two spectral lines a fraction of a nanometre apart can be resolved — and that is how the composition of stars is determined from their light.

questions.q: Explain polarisation, state Malus's law, and give two applications.
questions.solution:
**What it is.** In an unpolarised transverse wave the vibrations occur in **every** direction perpendicular to the travel. In a **plane-polarised** wave they are confined to one plane.

A **polaroid** transmits only the component along its transmission axis, and absorbs the rest.

**Unpolarised light through one polaroid** loses exactly half its intensity, since averaging $\cos^{2}\theta$ over all directions gives $\tfrac12$.

**Malus's law.** For already-polarised light of intensity $I_{0}$ meeting an analyser at angle $\theta$:

$I = I_{0}\cos^{2}\theta$

At $\theta = 90°$ the polaroids are **crossed** and nothing is transmitted.

**Applications.**

1. **Polarising sunglasses.** Light reflected from water or a wet road is partly polarised **horizontally**, so a lens with a vertical axis blocks most of the glare while passing ordinary light.

2. **Stress analysis.** Transparent plastic models placed between crossed polaroids show coloured fringes wherever the material is stressed, revealing where an engineering component will fail.

3. **LCD screens**, which work by rotating the plane of polarisation between two crossed polarisers.

4. **3D cinema**, projecting two images polarised at right angles so that each eye sees only one.

**A curiosity worth knowing:** three polaroids at $0°$, $45°$ and $90°$ transmit light, whereas the first and last alone transmit none. Adding a filter lets more light through — which is genuinely startling until Malus's law is applied twice.

questions.topic: Intensity and the inverse square law
questions.q: Explain why intensity falls as the inverse square of distance from a point source, and find the intensity at $6$ m if it is $100$ W/m$^{2}$ at $2$ m.
questions.solution:
**The reasoning.** A point source radiates equally in all directions, so at a distance $r$ the energy is spread over the surface of a sphere of area $4\pi r^{2}$.

$I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^{2}}$

The power is fixed; only the area over which it is spread changes.

**So $I \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$** — triple the distance and the same energy covers nine times the area, leaving a ninth of the intensity.

**The calculation.** Going from $2$ m to $6$ m is a factor of 3 in distance, so a factor of 9 in area:

$I = \dfrac{100}{9} = \mathbf{11.1}$ W/m$^{2}$

**Or formally:** $I_{1}r_{1}^{2} = I_{2}r_{2}^{2}$, giving $I_{2} = \dfrac{100 \times 4}{36} = 11.1$ ✓

**The assumption that must hold.** The source must be effectively a **point**, radiating uniformly, with no absorption or reflection on the way. A laser beam, which does not spread, obeys no such law.

**Where the same law appears:** gravitational and electrostatic fields, sound intensity, and radiation dose — which is why stepping back from a radioactive source is such an effective precaution. Doubling your distance quarters the dose.

**And since $I \propto A^{2}$**, the amplitude itself falls as $\dfrac{1}{r}$, not $\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$.
